lesson.title: The Full Mesh Analysis Toolkit: Meshes and Supermeshes Together
lesson.summary: Mesh analysis is the systematic combination of the mesh current method with supermeshes, handling ordinary resistor branches and current source branches within one solvable system.
lesson.body:
Just as nodal analysis is the node voltage method and the supernode technique working together, mesh analysis is the mesh current method and the supermesh technique working together as one complete procedure for any planar circuit. Most real multi loop circuits mix ordinary meshes, where every element in the loop has a well defined voltage to sum with KVL, and troublesome branches where a current source blocks that approach and forces a supermesh instead. Handling both correctly, in the same circuit, is the actual skill mesh analysis refers to.

The systematic version of the procedure is to first identify every mesh and assign each one a clockwise mesh current. Then scan the shared branches: if a branch shared between two meshes contains only resistors, write an ordinary KVL equation for each of those meshes normally. If a branch shared between two meshes contains a current source with nothing else in series, merge those two meshes into a supermesh, write one KVL equation around their combined outer boundary, skipping the source branch, and add one constraint equation stating that the difference of the two mesh currents equals the source value. Every mesh, ordinary or merged, contributes exactly the right number of independent equations to solve for every mesh current.

Consider a three mesh circuit. Mesh 1 contains a 16 volt source and a 2 ohm resistor, and shares a 3 ohm resistor with mesh 2, an entirely ordinary shared branch. Meshes 2 and 3 share a branch containing only a 2 amp current source, forcing them into a supermesh, with the source oriented so that I2 minus I3 equals 2 amps. Mesh 3 also contains its own 6 ohm resistor. The mesh 1 equation is negative 16, plus I1 times 2, plus (I1 minus I2) times 3, equals zero, which simplifies to 5I1 minus 3I2 equals 16. The mesh 2 and 3 supermesh equation, tracing the outer boundary of both and skipping the current source branch, is 3 times (I2 minus I1), plus 6 times I3, equals zero.

Solving this system gives I1 equals 5 amps, I2 equals 3 amps, and I3 equals 1 amp. Check mesh 1: negative 16, plus 5 times 2, plus (5 minus 3) times 3, equals negative 16 plus 10 plus 6, equals zero. Check the supermesh: 3 times (3 minus 5), plus 6 times 1, equals negative 6 plus 6, equals zero. Check the constraint: 3 minus 1 is 2 amps, matching the current source exactly. Every equation balances independently, confirming the solution.

With both nodal analysis and mesh analysis available as complete toolkits, choosing between them on a new circuit usually comes down to counting: a circuit with fewer independent nodes than meshes is normally faster by nodal analysis, and a circuit with fewer meshes than nodes is normally faster by mesh analysis, though either method, applied correctly, always arrives at the same currents and voltages in the end.
